app.title: Atmospheric Light Laboratory
app.subtitle: Why the sky is blue, why sunsets are red, and why a well is dark

header.resetTitle: Return every control to its starting value

star.title: Light source (star)
star.temperatureHelp: Sets the emitted spectrum through Planck's law. Hotter stars emit relatively more short-wavelength light.
star.elevationHelp: How high the star stands. Lowering it lengthens the path light takes through the air.
star.realisticInsolationHelp: Scales the incoming light by how far this world orbits from its star, so planets can be compared honestly.

atmosphere.title: Atmosphere
atmosphere.densityHelp: Multiplies every scattering coefficient. Zero means vacuum.
atmosphere.scaleHeightHelp: The height over which density falls by a factor of e. A larger H means a deeper, more gradual atmosphere.
atmosphere.aerosolHelp: Dust and droplets. These scatter almost all colours equally and mostly forwards.
atmosphere.aerosolTypeHelp: Swaps the suspended particles for a different mixture. Same gas, different grains: smog, desert dust or volcanic ash.
atmosphere.exponentHelp: The cross-section goes as 1/lambda^n. True Rayleigh scattering is n = 4. Drag it to 0 and the sky loses its colour.

observer.title: Observer
observer.positionHelp: Above zero you climb through the atmosphere. Below zero you descend a shaft while the air above you stays exactly the same.
observer.viewDirectionHelp: Measured from straight up. 0 degrees is the zenith, 90 degrees is the horizon.
observer.wellDepthHelp: Also sets how far down the position slider can travel.
observer.countShaftAirHelp: Off by default, so that descending changes geometry only. Switch it on to add the denser air that would really fill a deep shaft.
observer.zoomHelp: How much of the world the cross-section shows. Zoom out at a low Sun to see the chord its light has to cross - that length is why it is red. The mouse wheel works too.

rays.title: Ray simulation
rays.showScatteringHelp: Follow individual photons as they are deflected out of the beam.
rays.brightnessHelp: Multiplies the displayed brightness only. It never changes the computed physics or the hue.
rays.physicalMixHelp: Draw the families in the proportions the physics gives instead of the legible ones. Only about a sixth of the light crossing Earth’s air is scattered at all, so the picture fills with the unscattered beams that really do dominate it and the sky fan thins to almost nothing. Nothing measured changes — only what is drawn.
rays.scatterShareHelp: What share of the drawn paths are scattering events at all. This is a drawing budget, not a probability the physics uses: the measured colour divides by the directions it looked in, so it does not move when you change this.
rays.arrivingShareHelp: Of the scattering events drawn, the share turned towards the observer rather than away. Also a drawing budget — which of them really reach you is decided by the phase function, ray by ray.

canvas.title: Cross-section
canvas.skyStripHelp: The sky from horizon to horizon through the observer's own eyes. Black wedges are directions stopped by the shaft wall.
canvas.clickRay: Click any path to trace it step by step
canvas.rayLogEmpty: No ray selected. Click any ray in the cross-section.
canvas.verticalExaggerated: Vertical scale is compressed so that both the shaft and the whole atmosphere fit on one picture.
canvas.legendArriving: reaches you from where you are looking
canvas.legendOffView: reaches you from elsewhere in the sky
canvas.legendInCone: turns in view, but goes elsewhere
canvas.legendDirect: straight from the star, not to scale

spectrum.title: Spectrum
spectrum.empty: No light reaches the observer from this direction.

color.title: Perceived colour
color.computed: Computed from the spectrum through CIE 1931 XYZ, never chosen by hand.
color.blockedByWall: The shaft wall blocks this direction, so no light arrives at all.
color.darkness: Too little light to show a colour.
color.measured: What you see, measured from the rays
color.noneArrive: Not one ray comes down any of the {cast} directions in view.
color.noRays: No rays were traced in this direction.
color.measuredNote: Built only from the rays on screen, and it is the same calculation the strip under the picture uses - point the observer anywhere and the strip already shows this colour at that direction. The mix of the eight colours is the hue; how many of them there are, against how much sky the field of view still holds, is the brightness. Climbing leaves fewer rays because there is less air overhead to scatter; a shaft leaves less sky because the rock takes the directions. Too little light reads as dark. Brown means something else entirely: that you are facing the rock.
color.agreement: The integrator differs by dxy = {dxy}; brightness ratio {ratio} from {rays} rays.
color.belowOneRay: Less light than one ray stands for, across {cast} directions in view.
color.starInCone: The star is in your field of view: its disc is about {ratio} times brighter than the sky around it, so the bundle on the picture is not to scale and cannot be.

data.title: Physical quantities
data.advancedOnly: Switch to Advanced level to see the full readout.

daySky.see: The sky glows blue in every direction away from the star, while the star itself still looks close to white. Nothing here is painted blue: you are looking at sunlight that has been knocked sideways out of the beam by air molecules.
daySky.why: Rayleigh scattering has a cross-section proportional to 1/lambda^4. At 450 nm it is {ratio} times stronger than at 650 nm, so blue light is redirected into your eye far more often than red. The remaining beam keeps almost all of its red, which is why the star stays warm-white.

sunset.see: The star has dropped low and turned deep orange or red, and it has dimmed sharply. The colour change is not in the star, it is in the {airmass} times longer path its light now takes through the air.
sunset.why: Beer-Lambert extinction gives T(lambda) = exp(-tau(lambda)). Along this path tau is {tau450} at 450 nm but only {tau650} at 650 nm, so blue is stripped out almost completely while red survives. What you see is the leftover of the beam, not new red light.

twilight.see: The star is below the horizon. Direct light no longer reaches you, yet the sky is not black: it is lit only by air high above you that is still in sunlight.
twilight.why: The shadow of the planet has swallowed the lower atmosphere, so the scattering integral collects light only from the illuminated layers higher up. Single scattering already shows the effect; real twilight is deeper and more purple because photons bounce several times before arriving.

highAltitude.see: The sky above you has gone much darker and deeper in colour. The star has not changed and you have not left the atmosphere, but far less air remains overhead.
highAltitude.why: The column above you falls exponentially, C(z) = C(0) exp(-z/H). At {z} with H = {scaleHeight} only {columnPercent} of the air is left above you, so there is proportionally less material to scatter light towards your eye.

space.see: The sky is completely black although the star shines as brightly as ever, and it is now painfully sharp against the darkness. Light is streaming past you in enormous quantity; it simply has nothing to bounce off on its way to your eye.
space.why: The scattering integral has collapsed to zero because rho -> 0. Brightness of the sky needs a medium, not a source. This is why astronauts in daylight see a black sky, and why the same is true on the airless Moon.

airless.see: It is full daylight, the ground is brightly lit, and yet the sky directly overhead is black. Nothing is blocking the light - there is simply no air to scatter it.
airless.why: With rho = 0 every term in the scattering integral vanishes, while the direct transmission stays T = 1. A black sky proves the absence of a scattering medium, never the absence of light.

thinAir.see: The sky is almost black with the faintest hint of deep blue, and yet it is daytime and the ground is brightly lit. There is air here, there is simply far too little of it.
thinAir.why: Rayleigh scattering behaves exactly as it does on Earth and still favours blue by 1/lambda^4. But the optical depth is only {tau550}, so barely a thousandth of the passing light is scattered. The colour stays blue; only the brightness goes.

wellShallow.see: You have dropped into the shaft. The patch of sky through the mouth is exactly as bright and exactly as blue as it was outside - but it is now a small disc instead of the whole sky, and everything around you has darkened.
wellShallow.why: The air above you has not changed at all: C_atm is still C_atm(0). What changed is geometry. A ray leaving at zenith angle theta escapes only while tan(theta) <= R/d. Here that limit is {aperture}, leaving {solidAngle} of sky out of a full hemisphere.

wellDeep.see: Deep in the shaft it is nearly dark, yet the scrap of sky far above is still the same blue as at the surface. This is the key point: the darkness is not atmospheric, it is a hole you are looking through.
wellDeep.why: Radiance in the open direction is unchanged, but the illuminance follows the visible solid angle: E/E_open = sin^2(theta_max) = {ratio}. Compare this with climbing: at {z} up, the sky itself would be dimmer because the air column really did shrink.

dusty.see: The sky is pale ochre rather than blue, and the light is soft and diffuse. Larger particles are doing the scattering here, and they treat every colour almost alike.
dusty.why: Aerosols scatter with only a weak wavelength dependence (roughly 1/lambda^0 to 1/lambda^1) and a strongly forward-peaked Henyey-Greenstein lobe with g = {g}. Where the dust also absorbs blue more than red, as on Mars, the sky turns warm.

denseAtmosphere.see: The light down here is dim and heavily tinted. Very little of the original spectrum survives the journey to the surface.
denseAtmosphere.why: The optical depth is far above one, so exp(-tau) has extinguished the short wavelengths entirely. Note that a single-scattering model under-predicts the true brightness here: in reality photons scatter many times before arriving.

coldStar.see: The star is orange-red and the sky above it is a muted, dusky blue rather than a vivid one.
coldStar.why: Rayleigh scattering still prefers short wavelengths by 1/lambda^4, but the star emits little short-wavelength light for it to work on. The sky colour is the product of the scattering law and the source spectrum, not the scattering law alone.

hotStar.see: The star is blue-white and the sky is an intense deep blue, noticeably stronger than under a Sun-like star.
hotStar.why: A hot black body emits far more short-wavelength light, and the 1/lambda^4 law then amplifies that excess. Source spectrum and scattering law multiply together.

compare.controlsHelp: Which observer the left-hand panel drives. The other stays exactly where it is. Clicking a panel selects it too.
compare.enableHelp: Adds a second observer. Each gets their own simulation: their own rays, their own shaft, their own cross-section and their own strip of sky beneath it.
compare.note: The sliders below and the right-hand panel belong to this observer: {observer}.
compare.selected: selected - the controls drive this one
compare.title: Two observers

footer.modelNote: Light is followed from the star to one scattering event and then to the eye. Multiple scattering, refraction and ozone absorption are not modelled.
footer.sourceData: All physical data live in editable JSON files under /config.

histogram.title: Light the drawn rays deliver
histogram.help: The spectrum measured from the rays above, not computed from theory. Filled bars: light arriving at the observer, coloured from the viewing cone and grey from the rest of the sky. Dashed outline: the unscattered direct beam, scaled to its own peak because it is thousands of times brighter. The scale is held at the brightest sky seen so far, so climbing makes the bars fall.
